title: This Plastic Eats Itself in Just 6 Days!
summary:
Imagine a plastic wrapper that, instead of sitting in a landfill for hundreds of years, just disappears in less than a week. That's exactly what a team of scientists has created: a 'living plastic' that self-destructs in only six days! And the best part? It doesn't leave behind those tiny, harmful microplastics that get everywhere.

Here's the problem: we use a lot of plastic for just a few minutes—like a straw or a candy wrapper—but that plastic can stick around for centuries. So researchers asked, what if we could build a self-destruct button right into the plastic?

Their secret? Tiny sleeping bacteria called Bacillus subtilis. The scientists mixed these dormant spores into a common plastic called polycaprolactone (you might know it from 3D printing or some stitches doctors use). The spores stayed quiet and didn't weaken the plastic at all. But when the team wanted the plastic to disappear, they added warm, soupy nutrients and heated it to 122°F (50°C). That woke up the bacteria!

Once awake, the bacteria started making two special enzymes—think of them as tiny scissors. The first enzyme snipped the long plastic chains into shorter pieces. Then the second enzyme chewed those pieces down to the very basic building blocks. Because the two enzymes worked as a team, the plastic didn't just crumble into microplastics. It was completely broken down into harmless bits.

To prove it works in real life, the researchers built a wearable electronic patch from the living plastic. It did its job, and then, after two weeks, it was gone—fully degraded.

The team is now working on making this happen in water (where a lot of plastic pollution ends up) and with other types of plastics. So someday, your disposable fork might just vanish after you're done with it!
why_it_matters: One day your candy wrapper or plastic fork could vanish by itself after you use it, keeping parks and oceans cleaner.

background_read: Every year, the world produces over 400 million tons of plastic, but less than 10% is recycled. Most of it ends up in landfills or the ocean and stays there for centuries.
Scientists have been trying to create plastics that break down faster, using special chemicals or materials. Adding living bacteria is a completely new approach.
Polycaprolactone, the plastic used in the experiment, is already known to be biodegradable, but normally it takes months or years to break down.

perspectives.description: This invention could sharply reduce plastic trash and the tiny harmful bits that end up in animals and water.
The plastic must be kept in the right conditions until we want it to disappear—if it gets warm and wet too soon, it might start breaking down before we are done using it.
The technology still needs testing on different plastics and in water, so it may take many years before it is ready for everyday items.
